comment: The composite tail of the matrix: records, bytes at depth, typed maps and
nested composites. A SEPARATE table because these types have a separate

Both providers implement it — the C++ one header-first (its records are declared as C++ structs and the contract is derived from them), the Rust one contract-first — so this table has a differential like full_api does.
contract — the C++ cdylib backend's typeSupported() gate rejects records and
[bstr] by name, and its impl-header parser skips `struct` entirely, so a
header-first C++ provider cannot even declare a record. Putting them in
full_api would break test_fullapi_cpp's build rather than add a test.
that is a gap, not a design choice, and it closes when a C++ ext provider
exists. Until then these cells prove the contract works on one surface, not
that two surfaces agree.
Every expectation was MEASURED against the provider, not assumed.
OPTIONALITY (the `Optional/` and `hostile/Optional/` family). `?T` is
TWO-state: a value of T, or empty. Omitted and explicit-null are the SAME
state on decode and DIFFERENT on encode — empty is spelled by OMITTING the
key in a NAMED slot (a record field) and by null in a POSITIONAL one (a
method arg, a return), because a positional slot has no key to omit and the
arity must never change. The round trip is therefore CANONICALISING, not
identity, and several expectations below are deliberately NOT the argument
echoed back.
These are the one group in this table whose expectations were NOT measured
against a provider: they are derived from the contract, and they were
written before the implementation exists. Nothing in any generator reads
optionality yet (verified by executing them, see known-ext.json), so the
family is red on purpose and every cell that cannot pass is registered.

cases.why: a record reaches the Rust author as a real struct; the round trip goes through the generated to_json/from_json, so this passing means BOTH directions encode the fields
a bstr FIELD with bytes >= 0x80 — the reason records get hand-emitted to_json instead of a serde derive. See known-ext.json E1.
M1 seen through a record field: the provider rejects it with `expected integer at arg0.n, got number` — the field-path diagnostic is itself worth pinning
a record holding a record, a [tstr] and a [Record] — the recursion the generated encoders have to get right
codegen types [Record] but NOT {tstr: Record}, so this one arrives untyped — which is exactly why it is a separate cell
the type the C++ cdylib gate rejects by name; on the Rust side it is expressible, so the cell exists here
bytes two containers deep
a TYPED map, and its values carry the 64-bit range
an empty inner array is where an element type gets lost
the fire shim's bool return is a declared cell — the event case covers the payload, not this

PADDED base64 in a canonical tag, MEASURED: both providers decode it correctly on this path and re-emit the canonical unpadded form. Recorded because nothing covered padded input anywhere — every other bytes cell sends unpadded — and because the cdylib backend carries a SECOND byte decoder that bails on any non-alphabet character, returning an empty vector with no error. That decoder is not on this record-field path, so this cell is a regression guard for the codec unification rather than a baseline for a live defect. I predicted it would fail here and it did not; the expectation is what was measured.

a plain string where the contract says [bstr]. Both providers now ACCEPT it — the divergence that mattered is closed. Before the codec unification the C++ side refused, because a [bstr] ELEMENT went through the strict codec the cdylib backend emitted while a SCALAR bstr went through a lenient one: echoBytes("hi") succeeded and echoBytesList(["hi"]) threw, inside one module, for the same type. One function now.
Still pinned per provider because the ECHOED FORM differs, and that is not the same defect: C++ decodes to real bytes and re-emits the canonical tag, while Rust binds [bstr] as an untyped Value and echoes the input verbatim. A representation difference from an untyped binding, not a disagreement about what the value is.

the baseline: every optional field carries a VALUE, so nothing about optionality is exercised except that declaring it did not change the ordinary path. If this cell ever diverges from Record/nominal, optional support broke the case that was already working.

absent decodes to EMPTY — not an error, not a default — and empty re-encodes by OMITTING the key, because a named slot has a key to leave out and that is the one canonical spelling. The echo must come back with exactly one key. Two wrong answers this catches: {"required":"r","maybe":null,…}, i.e. empty spelled as null in a NAMED slot (a second wire form the contract does not have), and a rejection — which is what the Rust provider answers today, `expected string at arg0.maybe, got null`, because args::Ty::Record types a flag-optional field by its base type.

omitted and explicit-null are the SAME state on decode and DIFFERENT on encode, so the round trip is CANONICALISING rather than identity: null in, key gone out. This cell pins that asymmetry, and it is the reason the expectation is not simply the argument echoed back — a decoder that passed its input through verbatim would satisfy an identity check and still be wrong about which of the two spellings is canonical.

THE TRAP. "", 0 and the zero-length byte string are VALUES; only the single empty inhabitant (None / nullopt / invalid QVariant) is absence. A binding that reaches for a falsy test — `if (!v.maybe.empty())`, `if not v.count`, serde's skip_serializing_if — drops all three keys here while passing every other optional cell in this table. Present-and-empty must round-trip present.

optionality must not cost precision. uint64 max is the value that degraded to a double once nested (M1) and again through a record field (E3, closed by the codec unification); wrapping that same field in an optional adds a decode hop on every backend, and this is the cell that catches the hop reintroducing a double.

an absent NUMBER, isolated from the absent string: the failure mode here is a decoder that default-constructs a missing uint and emits "count": 0, which is indistinguishable from the real 0 that Optional/record/empty-value-is-not-absence sends on purpose. Absent must come back absent.

bytes ride their own canonical {"_bytes"} tag and have their own history of dying one level down (E1: every byte >= 0x80 became U+FFFD; E2: an empty nested bstr arrived as null). An OPTIONAL bstr wraps exactly that path in one more decode, and 0x00/0x80/0xFF is the payload that tells a real byte decode from a UTF-8 round trip.

the byte-string half of the empty/absent confusion, and the sharper one: an absent bstr must NOT arrive as {"_bytes": ""}. E2's history is that a zero-length nested bstr was already being turned into null in one direction, so the obvious repair — decode null to an empty vector — closes E2 and erases absence in the same edit. This cell is what stops that.

presence is PER ELEMENT. Three shapes in one array — fully present, fully absent, mixed with an explicit null — so a codec that decides key presence once for the whole list, or lets the first element template the rest (how a columnar or schema-sniffing encoder fails), cannot pass. It is also the only cell where the canonicalising round trip (element 3's null becoming an omitted key) happens at depth.
an empty list whose element type is a record with optional fields: an empty array is where an element type gets lost ([[int]]/empty-inner), and an optional element type is one more thing to lose.

the `?T` TYPE-KIND spelling, which spec.md:179,184-185 binds to the same meaning as the `? name: T` field flag that Opt uses. The two must emit identical code; today they do not even agree at runtime — a flag-optional field is validated against its base type while `?tstr` falls to args::Ty::Any and is not validated at all — which is why both spellings are in one contract.

a POSITIONAL slot has no key to omit and the arity must never change, so empty is spelled null — in the argument and in the return. Two independent blockers today, both registered: the py driver cannot SEND this argument (logoscore-py's _arg_to_str falls through to str(None), so the daemon receives the literal string "None"), and a null RETURN is the failure token further up (logos_json_convert turns null into an invalid QVariant and core_service reports METHOD_FAILED), so an empty optional return is currently indistinguishable from a failed call.

the positional twin of Optional/record/empty-value-is-not-absence: "" is a present value and must come back "", not null. A binding that models `?tstr` as "a string, possibly empty" — the natural shortcut in any language whose string type has no null — collapses the two states exactly here.

R4, and the cell a lazy fix cannot pass: optional widens the domain by exactly ONE inhabitant (empty); it does not disable type checking. 42 is neither a tstr nor empty, so it must be REJECTED — not coerced, and not quietly treated as empty. Today the Rust provider ACCEPTS it and echoes 42 because ty_descriptor's catch-all makes `?tstr` args::Ty::Any, and both C++ paths spell Optional as an untyped QVariant/any for the same reason. Modelling `?T` as `any` passes every other optional cell in this table and fails only this one.

R4 through a field path — the diagnostic should name arg0.maybe. This cell PASSES today by accident (args::Ty::Record types `? maybe: tstr` as Tstr and rejects the int), and that is precisely why it is worth writing down: the obvious implementation of optional decoding, o.get("maybe").and_then(|v| v.as_str()), turns a present-but-wrong value into None — it would make every absent-field cell pass and REGRESS this one.

the liberal decode is scoped to OPTIONAL slots. A missing REQUIRED field stays an error, unchanged. This guards the over-broad fix: making the record decoder tolerate absence everywhere would turn all four absent-field cells green and silently delete the difference between `required: tstr` and `? required: tstr`.

the other half of that guard: an explicit null in a REQUIRED slot is still an error, even though the identical token is a legal empty one field over. Absent and null are one state; which slot they land in is what decides whether the state is legal.
